subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ALLOCATION OF INVESTMENT FUND

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ALLOCATION OF INVESTMENT FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement on the Canada Pension Plan investment fund.
Under the Canada Pension Plan, all funds received but not required at the end of each month to meet expenses and payments of benefits during the following three months are transferred to the Canada Pension Plan investment fund for the purchase of securities of the provinces or the government of Canada. These are special non-marketable securities, with terms of up to 20 years.
The allocation for purchases of provincial securities by the Canada Pension Plan investment fund is proportionate to the amounts of contributions paid in each province. Any balance not taken up by the provinces, together with funds collected in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, must be invested in special non-marketable securities of the government of Canada. The securities issued for this purpose by the government of Canada are subject to the same conditions as those issued by the provinces.
The first funds were available for investment by the Canada Pension Plan investment fund at the end of February. These were derived from contributions paid in January and amounted to $34,852,909. Provincial treasurers have been advised that the amounts available for the purchase of their securities up to and including March 10, 1966, are as follows:	Newfoundland, $655,000; Prince
Edward Island, $108,000; Nova Scotia, $1,248,000; New Brunswick, $972,000; Ontario, $20,110,000; Manitoba, $2,077,000; Saskatchewan, $1,432,000; Alberta, $3,064,000; British Columbia, $5,085,000.
If the provinces take up the above amounts as expected, the amount available for the purchase of securities of Canada will be $101,909. The rate of interest applicable to these securities, as determined by the Minister of Finance under the act, is 5.29 per cent. Interest is payable semi-annually.
A statement was issued in the form of a press release on February 4 giving a preliminary forecast of the amounts which might be available to the investment fund for the purchase of provincial securities. Because of lags in the receipt of contributions and the need to deduct administrative expenses which had already accrued, the amount available for investment in this first month was somewhat below the preliminary forecast.
I am making this statement, Mr. Speaker, because I believe there is some interest among members in this initial allocation of pension plan funds. In future the provinces will be notified directly of the amounts available, and I do not intend to make such an announcement each month.

subtopic: RECOGNITION OF CHINESE GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
1. Canada recognized the Government of the Republic of China as the de jure government of China on December 20, 1928. On that date, the United Kingdom minister in China, with the authorization of the Canadian Government, undertook an exchange of notes with the Chinese National Government which had the effect of renouncing the rights of Canada to benefit by the provisions of existing treaties limiting the right of China to settle her national customs tariff or to impose tonnage dues. It was the express intention of the then Canadian Government that this exchange of notes constitute recognition by Canada of the Government of the Republic of China. A Canadian Legation, later raised to the status of an Embassy, was opened in China in 1942, but closed after the National Government left the mainland to establish itself on Formosa in 1949. The Canadian Government continues to recognize the Government of the Republic of China at its present seat of government.

GRANT TO PEACE RESEARCH ABSTRACTS
speechtext: Has the government received representations concerning a grant to Peace Research Abstracts and, if so, what response has been made to such representations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GRANT TO PEACE RESEARCH ABSTRACTS
speechtext:
The government received a request from the Canadian Peace Research Institute on October 8, 1965 for a grant of $35,024 to assist the work of Peace Research Abstracts in the year 1966. I replied on January 24 as follows:
The government is sympathetic to the objectives of the CPRI and regards the Peace Research Abstracts as a constructive and useful publication. We have also been happy to note the decision by UNESCO to grant assistance for the publication of the Abstracts. We also believe, however, that projects of this kind are best supported by private means or, if they qualify, by the Canada Council, which as you know does make grants available to scholars or organizations concerned with the social sciences. The fact is that the Department of External Affairs does not subsidize research or publications in this field, although we do help the United Nations Association of Canada because it performs tasks which are directly related to publicizing the objectives of the United Nations and Canada's part therein. You will, I am sure, appreciate that a grant for the publication of Peace Research Abstracts would be likely to attract requests for the support of similar projects by other institutions or individuals. There is no legislation or machinery which would enable us to evaluate such requests and to reach sensible decisions on them. I do not rule out the possibility that this situation may change. I am aware for example that the governments of Norway and Sweden have approached this matter differently. For the present, however, and for the reasons given I regret not being able to respond favourably to your request. Please be assured that we shall continue to be glad to extend informal assistance and advice to the CPRI whenever you consider this useful or appropriate.

subtopic: NATIONAL EMPLOYMENT COMMITTEE RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
1.	At its 91st meeting, on August 31 and September 1, 1965, the national employment committee passed one resolution respecting personnel matters of the national employment service, including the written test.
2.	(a) The resolution was addressed to Hon. Allan J. MacEachen, then Minister of Labour, (b) Yes. (c) The resolution was as follows:
That the national employment committee is pleased to learn of the substantial upward revision of salary rates for employment officers as a result of the introduction of a new series of employment service officer, and the upgrading of the basic qualifications of applicants for such positions. The committee also welcomes the decision to establish 948 new positions in the National Employment
Questions
Service. It is felt that these changes should greatly improve the quality of the staff generally, and the efficiency of the National Employment Service. The committee notes with concern the fact that the filling of vacant position has been frozen pending the development of a test and appraisal program, and urges that a decision in this matter be arrived at as quickly as possible, so that the already excessive number of vacancies will not result in a serious impairment of the service. The national employment committee also notes the intention of the Civil Service Commission to require present NES staff to pass a written test in order to gain access to the new series. This procedure, we understand, is causing considerable unrest among the employees and it is the view of the national employment committee that the stipulation with respect to the written tests of present employees should be considered and that the appraisal program for entry into the new series be administered so that decisions affecting present employees will be based upon their performance in the National Employment Service. The national employment committee is strongly of the opinion that the National Employment Service should be represented on the body responsible for appraisal of present staff.
Following consideration of the resolution, the Minister of Labour informed the Chairman of the national employment committee that an objective test was necessary because previous experience had clearly indicated that it was not sufficient, in introducing a major personnel change such as the employment service officer series, to rely solely on appraisal of past performance. The chairman was subsequently informed of the precise role of the written test as an aid in the evaluation of candidates, and also informed that all the appraisal boards responsible for these evaluations would include representation from the NES.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
1. The recreation hall at Cavendish in Prince Edward Island national park was erected in 1950 to provide a centre for recreation and the entertainment of park visitors. At that time, overnight camping and picnicking were permitted at Cavendish beach near the junction of Cawnpore lane and the Gulf Shore Road. Activities carried on under a recreational director included film showings, square and round dances, camp fires and sing-songs and a daytime program for children, including games.
With the development of a new campground at New London bay and the termination of camping at the Cavendish beach site, a recreation hall at that location had outlived its original purpose, and in the latter years of its operation, the evening programs were frequently interrupted by rowdyism and special policing measures were necessary. These disturbances were mainly related to the attendance of persons from points some distance from the park. Furthermore, the officer in charge of recreational programs in 1963 received requests to curtail or rearrange the
March 2, 1966

dates of dances so as to not conflict with those held by organizations located in communities adjacent to but outside the park. These included the Rustico recreational committee, New Glasgow junior farmers, and Stanley Bridge Hall committee.
Following the development of a national park interpretation and the appointment of a seasonal park naturalist, the former recreation program at Cavendish beach was discontinued. The park interpretation program is directed principally from the Dalvay region which contains the park headquarters. Activities are carried on in both the Dalvay and Cavendish areas with emphasis on attracting the park campground populations.
With the change in the park emphasis to an appreciation of the natural features of the park, and the appointment of a park naturalist to develop a new program, the recreation hall was relocated from the congested area at Cavendish beach to the new Cavendish camp ground. It seems that the recreational function that the hall served in its previous location can best be carried out by private enterprise outside the national park.
2.	As a centre for the park naturalist's interpretation programs including lectures and films in inclement weather and as a focal point for the commencement of conducted trail outings.
3.	The Honourable J. Watson MacNaught, Summerside, P.E.I., Mr. John C. Mullally, Souris, P.E.I., Mr. R. S. Humphreys and the Cavendish Resort Association.
4.	An interpretative program is being carried out in the park this summer. Primarily educational, this program is also recreational in character. It endeavours to show and present to the public points of interest, gives facts of natural history that the public might not otherwise know about, and provides recreation, educational and informal instruction to the park visitors giving a better understanding not only of the park and its natural features but also of the purpose which the park serves. It consists of talks accompanied by films, conducted trips and a self-guiding interpretative trail.

Certainly the policies of the government are geared to the end that the minimal income of the viable economic farm unit will be of the same measure, of the same nature and in the same economic bracket.
With those brief words, Mr. Chairman, and with the hope that our policies will be successful and that we will get the co-operation of the house, as I know we will, in bringing about these effective policies when they are before us. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first I should like to thank the minister for the courtesy he has shown in making a statement. On behalf of the opposition I should like to thank him particularly for his deliberate course of action in staying completely away from the partisan political role. I am sure he will find that,

because of his determined course in this respect his estimates will receive ready acceptance from this side of the house.
One of the important aspects in the agricultural field in the last few years relates to a feeling by the farmers of this great nation that partisan politics have been creeping into the department in such a way that its efficiency can be crippled to some degree. I am not going to elaborate on this in a partisan manner because I hope to stay absolutely away from partisanship, but I do wish to point out three examples where this was very evident.
In Ontario the sugar beet growers were very much disturbed last fall by the fact that subsidy cheques which they had earned and which were owing to them were delayed for many weeks. All interrogation of the minister and the department by members on this side of the house failed to procure any kind of statement why this situation existed. Is it not strange that on the Saturday preceding the last election, after weeks of delay, thousands of dollars in subsidy cheques poured into the hands of the sugar beet growers not because of the benevolence of the government but because the money was owing to these farmers. This cannot be regarded as a coincidence because the cheques did not arrive on the usual staggered basis but were directed to all mail routes so that they arrived simultaneously.
The farmers of the area concerned took a very dim view of this because they felt that not only were partisan politics involved but pressure had also been brought to bear on the Department of Agriculture to make such a course of action possible. I want to congratulate the minister, however, because he stayed out of party politics, which was not the course of action followed by his predecessor. I am sure one little incident will bear out what I mean in this regard.
I posed a question in the house to the previous minister of agriculture and he took the question as notice. I had no objection to that because it was his privilege to do so. However, I object very strenuously to the fact that having taken my question as notice his office telephoned the next morning to the local Liberal M.L.A. and gave him the answer before it had even been given to me in the house. That gentleman then telephoned the local radio station which in turn made it available to everyone over the air. Surely that is partisan politics.
I should like to outline one more incident of this type and then leave this subject. I was

most unhappy and disturbed when I visited a great farm community group who wished to present their views to the government as to what should be done in the field of agriculture because it appeared to me that at that meeting they were combing their membership for known government party workers to present their brief. They did not feel their views would be listened to unless they were presented by known party workers. That is a sad state of affairs.
1 wish now to congratulate the minister on his appointment to office. Following his appointment there were two questions which arose in the minds of farmers across the country. The first related to the fact that the hon. gentleman appointed to the ministry was a member of the House of Commons for an eastern constituency. What was the reaction to that appointment? I am delighted to say that the reaction so far as I was concerned, and as far as I could ascertain from a large group of farmers, was that they had no concern at all whether the minister was from the east or from the west as long as he delivered the goods, because that is what they are interested in.
The next question was related to his background. Was he a farmer? The farmers did not care whether or not he was a farmer. Farmers today are interested in what is ahead of them and what is to come. They want to know how the minister will receive their delegations, whether he will be sympathetic and what action he will take. They want to know whether he will direct the Department of Agriculture to assist them. That is the interest of the farmers of this country, not whether he is a farmer. I am very pleased that they are not interested in that aspect.
We could not of course expect the minister, who is new to one of the greatest departments of government and no doubt has a tremendous amount to learn, to make a policy statement today, especially in view of the fact he is dealing with the estimates of his predecessor. However, one of the things that has troubled us about the Department of Agriculture during the last three years is that there has never been a definite statement of policy made by the minister of agriculture, the Prime Minister or anyone on that side of the house.
Today there was no indication of appreciation of or concern for some of the main problems that face the agricultural industry
March 2, 1966

at this time. We were hoping that the minister would give some indication of government thinking in this regard. One of the big problems in the agricultural field today relates to the dairy industry. What lies ahead for that industry? The new year, so far as the dairy industry is concerned, is just ahead of it. What action does the government contemplate and where is it going in this area? I do not choose to deal with dairy problems because speakers who will follow me will do so in some detail but I wanted to point out that there is a problem in this regard.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Another problem is the extreme poverty that exists in some rural areas today. Farmers are faced, as are all other Canadian citizens today, with a tremendous increase in the cost of living that far exceeds the increase in their incomes. They are also faced with the ever-increasing cost of farm machinery and have to contend with this problem. Another problem that is becoming increasingly important and vital to the farmers is the lack of skilled, semi-skilled or even day labour to assist them. The lack of farm labour has very serious implications.
We are also concerned about the lack of any evidence of an over-all agricultural policy on the part of the government. I do not intend to spend the time allocated to me in dwelling on what the Conservative party did when it was in office. We made attempts in two basic areas. We started on a deliberate dairy policy for the nation as a whole. There are some indications that the government is carrying this policy even farther. We established through ARDA and other programs a policy designed to aid farmers, especially those in the more rural areas where poverty has become so evident.
We set up ARDA for this purpose, and there are indications that the government is carrying this project even farther. But we on this side of the house are concerned about the fact that most of the policies of the government have been based on policies that we established. They increased farm income; they increased farm loans; they increased Farm Credit Corporation loans; they made it possible through syndicates to buy more machinery. We had worked on these policies which were set up to help farmers.
However, Mr. Chairman, unfortunately conditions have changed to such a degree that in many instances these measures have created hardship. Increasing the amount of farm
Supp ly-A griculture
loans did three things. First, it did not solve anything. It put farmers deeper in debt because their obligations were increased. Second, since it gave young farmers more money with which to buy land a greater demand for farm land developed and its price increased. Third, when the machinery companies found that farmers had more money to spend, they took advantage of this fact and raised the price of farm machinery to some extent. So this policy did not settle anything. It did not meet any of the main problems it was designed to meet.
We in the opposition believe that the policy which was designed to help farmers in their distress in 1955, 1956 and 1957, and which we feel was successful, is not an absolute policy and should not be followed today. Conditions have changed vastly since that time and we believe a new policy should be introduced that will meet the conditions of farming today.
Hon. members on both sides of the house have to rely to a marked degree on recommendations made by farm groups which make a study of basic conditions in the industry. The farm groups have made recommendations. The Standing Committee on Agriculture listened to these groups. The groups made recommendations to the committee and the committee made a report to the government last March, but not one single policy advocated in the report has up to this time been introduced by the government.
One recommendation very dear to the hearts of the farmers in my area was that the feed subsidy paid by the government on the freighting of western feed grain into eastern Canada be paid in respect of feed grains moving from Ontario into traditional markets in the east. This was asked for and was recommended by the committee but it was turned down by the government. No doubt it was turned down by the government for what they felt to be good and sufficient reason, but I do not understand their reason and I hope at a later date to have the opportunity to debate this very important matter.
We are also very concerned about the Department of Agriculture as a department. Our great Department of Agriculture is made up of men who for the most part have spent all their lives in some field of agriculture. The Department of Agriculture has through the years established an international reputation not only with regard to assessing problems in agriculture on a day to day basis but

March 2, 1966
Supply-Agriculture
in assessing the future of agriculture and providing measures to meet tomorrow's situations.
The department has evolved various agricultural projects which have made farming so successful. We have increased production and have adopted new practices, thanks to the Department of Agriculture. We have extended the areas in which various crops can be grown, thanks to the work of the Department of Agriculture.
But what alarms us very much today is the fact that the government has taken the Department of Agriculture and divided it into several departments which have been placed under different ministers. This is of extreme concern to those of us who are so vitally concerned with agriculture, because it is directly contrary to the action of the Department of National Defence which has said that by amalgamation it has been able to cut down expense and increase efficiency. We want to know whether splitting up the Department of Agriculture will increase expense and cut down efficiency. Surely this does not work both ways. We believe we shall have to take a long look at this problem and find out exactly what the reaction is across the country to the division of the department. If the division of the Department of Agriculture will increase efficiency and help farmers and farm organizations, then we in the opposition will give credit to the government for its action, but until we have some tangible proof that it will have this effect we shall view the whole operation with suspicion.
We hope that the government will live up to its intention of placing before the Standing Committee on Agriculture the estimates of the Department of Agriculture for the next fiscal year. We shall ask the minister whether this is the intention of the government because we want departmental officials to appear before the committee in order that we may ask them questions. We do not want to persecute them but to find out if they are hampered in any way in their activities. We want to know whether they feel they have enough money for research in agriculture, which is so important today and so necessary for the future of the industry. We want to know whether they have the facilities with which to work. We want to know whether they are given the opportunity to attend agricultural functions and meetings throughout the world because agriculture is of world wide importance now and is not limited to Canada. We want to find out just what the

policy of the government is, in what direction they are going and whether they are providing the necessary funds and opportunities to carry out this policy.
We have been alarmed during the last two years when ministers of agriculture have stood in their place and announced that action had been taken in regard to agriculture which would result in the saving of millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money. We all like to save money, but anyone engaged in the industry knows that drastic cut-backs by the government in this field mean that some section of the industry has to suffer an economic squeeze. We do not want to see this happen.
There is one other matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister in regard to the position of agriculture today. I wish to commend some of the provincial governments for taking an absolutely new look at the problems of agriculture and approaching them from a new angle. Some provincial governments are approaching these problems from the viewpoint that agriculture should encompass every phase of food production and use from the producer to the consumer and should be under one department. I am one of those who feel this is a step in the right direction.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Surely we should know if the consumer is paying too much for a commodity. We should know if the primary producer is receiving too little for a commodity. We should know the amount of money it costs to take primary products from the farmer to the ultimate consumer. If all this information were available within the Department of Agriculture, we would then be in a position to look at the entire picture and perhaps not only make food more readily available to the consumer but through efficiency make our farmers more competitive in world markets. Perhaps we could reduce some expenses that are hurting the primary producer.
There are two other aspects of agriculture that I feel are in dire trouble. I do not believe the government is approaching them from the right angle. We have heard of the government proposition to buy submarginal farm land, convert it and sell it back to farmers. I do not believe this approach is feasible. I think it is too costly and I do not believe it will achieve the result desired.
When we look at the program to help farmers we must realize that today there is a
March 2, 1966

new type of farmer who is increasing in numbers. I refer to the farmer who makes only part of his living from the land where his home is situated and part of his living working in industry or from some other position. In other words, he is a part time farmer. We must realize that such farmers are not only here but are entitled to the opportunity to earn a living in this way. They are entitled to help. We must recognize that this type of farmer is a growing part of our agricultural picture and must receive every consideration.
Surely there must be some other way of helping a farmer than buying his land and moving him away. Perhaps another method would be the building of new roads into certain inaccessible areas, thus bringing in tourists, people who would build new cottages and create a need for more labour. A new motel, a new marina or a fishing resort might be developed. This is the sort of thing into which we should be looking now rather than curtailing the activities of the man who is making a living off the farm.
There is another change taking place which I do not believe most men engaged in agriculture expected. I refer to the dire plight of the large mechanized farmer, the man who has specialized or taken part in vertical integration. These large operators need help badly because they cannot find men to operate their extensive holdings. They have made tremendous capital expenditures on machinery but because of the labour picture are unable to obtain labourers to run the machines which are becoming ever more complicated. In addition, these large operators find they can no longer engage competent managers. As a result there is great inefficiency and a tremendous rise in costs. They thought they would make money because of their large production but they find the reverse is true and because of the extensiveness of their holdings they are suffering even greater hardship.
These are the things into which we should be looking. What can we do to help these men? More farm labour is going to have to be brought into this country in order to plant and harvest the large crops. We are going to have to comb every place in Canada where there is an excess of labour and try to engage these people on a seasonal basis for those areas where labour is needed. I feel that this method alone will not provide the answer to our labour problems. Other steps will have to be taken. I am encouraged to know that we
Supply-Agriculture
are not alone in our concern. Members in all parts of the house are not only concerned about the situation but are taking concerted action to do something about it.
Finally I should like to say this to the minister. He is from eastern Canada and is therefore in a position to assess and be familiar with the problems of eastern Canada. He is a new minister without an agricultural background and probably has the advantage of having no preconceived ideas. He can listen to the officials of his department and take the advice of the great farm delegations that come here periodically. He can assess the tremendous needs of agriculture today and by directives can formulate a policy that will once more put the agricultural industry of Canada into a position of being envied throughout the world as once was the case.
Unfortunately this image has been fading lately because we are not delivering the goods. In my honest opinion, one of the great areas in which this country is falling behind is in the field of research development and sale of agricultural products throughout the world. Tremendous steps are being taken in this direction by other countries. There have been tremendous developments in the production of food. Make no mistake about it, Mr. Chairman, in the next few years we in this country will see the time when food and clean water will be as valuable as many of the base metals. We might just as well face this fact now and try to take steps to take advantage of the situation by keeping our water clean and providing the necessary agricultural commodities that will sell throughout the world. We can only do this by planning and by the work of our agricultural technicians. I have visited establishments that are only waiting for the word to go and they will give us the necessary products to sell. If we do not sell our products, if we do not make them competitive, we are going to find ourselves in the position where the nations of this world, by the use of carbon and other base materials, will possess synthetic foods produced through chemical processes and will not need our products to the degree they do today.
Let us provide the products they need. We have such a golden opportunity. Many millions of people in the world are starving to death because of a lack of protein and carbohydrates, two essential food elements which we have in excess in this country. Some success has been achieved in processing

March 2, 1966
Supply-Agriculture
these elements in a form in which they can be shipped to all needy countries. We are going to have to have a program, we are going to have to barter, we are going to have to exchange goods for goods. This is the sort of program the Department of Agriculture should be adopting. The department should ascertain what we need from these countries. Let us trade with these countries. They do not want extended credit; they want to trade. Certainly they have some things we can use.
I feel the time has come when we should move into this field. Let us find out what they can use. Let us provide it for them at a price they can afford.
This government has used subsidies and marketing schemes as a means of answering farm problems. Previous governments have done the same thing. This is a common practice of provincial administrations in the field of agriculture. The men who are engaged in agriculture have come to the definite conclusion that subsidies and marketing schemes do aid in times of dire trouble but that they are not an answer to all agricultural problems today. We have to take a new look at these problems. We have to move into new fields. Agriculture is an industry with tremendous horizons. Now is the time to move into new fields. The only way we can do this is to go to our technicians in the industry who, I say with utter conviction, are second to none in this world, and give them an opportunity to place Canada in the forefront. Let them tell us what the problems are. Let them suggest solutions and let us back them with our support and taxpayers' money. I assure you it is my conviction that this approach will be cheaper to the taxpayer in the long run.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize the minister has been very brief in his remarks in introducing the estimates of his predecessor and I do not blame him for this for two reasons. First of all, the money is pretty well gone and, second, there is really nothing creditable in the operations and stewardship of the previous minister of agriculture. None of the problems he faced originally were solved and the condition of agriculture now is no better than when he was first appointed minister.
Whether or not the new minister from eastern Canada will change this state of affairs I do not know, but let him remember that if he fails he may be pensioned off to the

other place, which perhaps would not be a bad thing either. However, the Canadian public are looking to the federal government for assistance which they have not been getting and I personally am looking to the new Minister of Agriculture to consider some of the problems he now faces.
I was very pleased to hear him be so brash as to say that much of the responsibility for the problem in moving grain in western Canada rested entirely upon the shoulders of the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway, who had failed to provide box cars for the movement of wheat when requested to do so. The fact that he is not going to do anything about it is not necessarily his fault but the fault of his friends in the cabinet who are failing to take the necessary steps so apparent to the new minister who knows the problem and sees the solution. When the officials advise him that you cannot force the Canadian Pacific Railway to provide box cars and that you cannot provide larger quotas for some of the points shipping grain, then they make the problem even more difficult for the minister. However, I hope he will be able to continue taking that fresh look which he apparently took of some of the problems which have faced us over the years in western Canada which though not yet solved are not without solution.
In speaking on the estimates last year I made reference to a problem which had developed in Ontario and in particular in my part of Ontario. It is one which last year caused a disaster. I have on the order paper a bill to introduce legislation to govern, license and regulate the operation of rainmaking machines. No doubt each hon. member has his own opinion whether or not rainmaking machines do produce rain, but in any case both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Forestry are aware of the fact that a superabundance of rain fell last year in the northern part of Ontario creating a problem completely foreign to the Minister of Agriculture who comes from an area which suffered to about the same degree for exactly the opposite reason.
The farmers in my area believe that the rainmaking equipment used by the Ontario Department of Lands and Forests, the Ontario Hydro and by private pulp and paper companies had a great deal to do with the fact that it rained almost every day last year and destroyed a large percentage of the hay and grain crop in my area as well as almost
March 2, 1966

all the seed produced in the area which amounts to about half the total production in Ontario. It is interesting to note that the Ontario government spent a quarter of a million dollars on the installation of rainmaking equipment in the minister's riding last year to produce rain. Whether or not there can be compatibility in the use of such equipment in different areas is a moot point and one which will be kicked around at farmers' meetings probably for the next couple of years.
I believe that the Department of Agriculture should give some consideration to the various aspects of rainmaking and should investigate the potential of this operation. If it works in areas where there is a drought it would be advantageous. If it works in areas which have an abundance of rain, then I suggest that probably some compensation should be made available to the farmers. In my area between 50 per cent to 80 per cent of the hay crop was submarginal. This was not because we did not have a good crop. We had a bumper crop. The same was true of grain. However, it rained all through the haying season and most of the hay that was cut stayed on the ground. Also, a lot of it was not even cut and much of it put into the barns was not fit to feed to stock and in many cases was dangerous as feed owing to its condition.
A somewhat similar situation exists with regard to grain. I estimate that in Timis-kaming the farmers received something less than a 50 per cent return on their grain. In the Cochrane district they probably received less than 30 per cent.
The reason I raise this matter is that the federal government has been interested over the years in crop insurance. They have also been interested in natural disasters. They introduced the prairie farm rehabilitation scheme and have given assistance in cases of disaster for some time. In Ontario assistance is given with the co-operation of the provincial government but for the last few years the Ontario government has not looked farther than the edge of Toronto. If the grass is green on the lawn of the parliament buildings, then agriculture in the province must be in fairly good shape.
How little attention is paid to northern Ontario is seen by the fact that the situation to which I have referred became so acute that it was made an election issue, and the Prime Minister of Canada became involved and made all sorts of silly promises, as did 23033-131
Supply-Agriculture
others. The Ontario department decided to apply the same drought program in my area as was applied in the Renfrew area, which means that coupons were issued to the farmers to enable them to buy grain and hay. Assistance is provided up to $30 per ton for feed grain and $15 per ton for hay. The difficulty is that no hay is available. Most of the farmers have insufficient money to make up the difference in the cost of grain, which is about $30 to $35 per ton in addition to the government subsidy. I think the minister will agree that this is not good legislation. I think he will agree that further assistance must be given to these farmers.
I had hoped that the Minister of Agriculture would be from the province of Quebec. While many people have spoken of backward conditions over the years in the province of Quebec, anyone who looks at Quebec today will find that agriculture in the province is much more advanced so far as assistance to farmers is concerned and certainly more advanced than agriculture in the province of Ontario, of which I have some knowledge. I was quite surprised and pleased to find that in the last throne speech in the province of Quebec another $9 million was allocated to the Lake St. John disaster area to meet the situation that arose in 1964-65, whereas in Ontario the government is willing to make only a 50 per cent contribution to the livestock program to keep cows alive during the winter so they can go on pasture in the spring. It is an animal-humanitarian type of program which really does not do much to help the farmers stay in business.
When the Prime Minister visited my area during the election campaign I was surprised to find him talking about the fact that the government was going to buy a number of farms in different areas, take them over and operate them for a while and when they became operating units sell them back to the farmers. I suggest that perhaps the crop disasters in my area have helped the government considerably because it looks as though a lot of these farms will become available without the government having to buy them.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
It is a type of crisis prevalent throughout the country and particularly in my area. In Canada we are faced with a type of agricultural disaster. Farmers are no longer able to carry on for any period of time because they are working on a very close margin. I am sure the minister knows these facts. I am not

March 2, 1966
Supp ly-A gricul ture
sure what he is going to do about his officials when he brings farm problems to their attention. I believe that with very few exceptions there will be very little change so long as the officials of the department have their present attitude, which seems to be a fairly political one, as a result of which they act in such a manner that they will just get by.
I think that many officials in the Department of Agriculture will have to look at the effects of redistribution because from that will come changes that the officials will have to take into consideration. There will be a great shake-up in the Department of Agriculture when there is no support for the program which they have been carrying on for some time. I repeat that agriculture is in a very serious crisis. It is in a state of crisis not only respecting disasters, because the department helps nobody in disasters, but is in a state of crisis in many other areas.
I spoke to a man the other day who indicated that he had gone over the books of a young farmer who had spent considerable money in the buying of a large farm unit in which he had combined a number of smaller farms. He had gone into the meat production field, found himself in serious difficulty because of the lack of crop last year, had sold his cattle at a very large loss, had extended himself into the dairy products field, and now finds that he is plagued with the same problems as other dairy farmers are. Those problems arise from the lack of a dairy program in Ontario. Consequently he finds that he is selling about 25 per cent of his production on a quota giving him $25 a hundred while three quarters of his production is going at the surplus price of $2.85 which is considerably below his cost of production.
This farmer is going to be out of business very shortly unless something is done. We have talked of $4 milk in the house. A dairy commission has now been established in the province of Ontario and I am hopeful, as are the farmers, that the result in a short time will be the establishment of a unit price of $4 across the province so that all dairy producers will receive this price. I think assistance from the federal government will be required. If the program I have referred to is not successful then you will find we will have sr situation with considerable competition across the borders between provinces and surplus milk being dumped from one province into another and so on. For instance, it might be found that casein is being dumped in one
[Mr. Peters.l
province and fluid milk in another, or it might be found that butter is being dumped in one province and cheese is being moved in the opposite direction.
It is interesting to note that the provincial government of Quebec has a 25 cent subsidy that has helped to create a problem with respect to movements of milk across the border. This, I think, is a field to which the minister will have to give consideration.
If agriculture as a whole is to survive, then the prices of agricultural products must rise. The cost squeeze on farmers must be reduced. At the same time there is another point that farmers are not taking into consideration but that the minister and the government must take into consideration. I refer to the unholy rise in the price of every commodity that people eat. Almost all these commodities are agricultural products. In this country we could very easily get into a position where consumers would not be able to buy the commodities that are produced, no matter how high the subsidy is. In this country as in the United States, we could find ourselves in a predicament where the government will have to provide subsidies to keep land out of production. If that were to happen, I think the failure of the federal Department of Agriculture would be known to everyone and it would be almost complete.
The farmers will agree, I think, that if the country has to pay a subsidy to keep land out of production something must be badly wrong with the whole scheme of things. Something must be wrong when you deny starving peoples of the world the commodities which would have been grown had land not been taken out of production.
Many problems face Canada today in the agricultural field. I am not one of those who particularly want the agricultural estimates to go before the agricultural committee this year. I am not interested in farm machinery prices being discussed before the agricultural committee. I say that because I have not, nor has any other member of the house, any assurance that anything will happen with respect to any thing discussed before that committee. In my office I have a thick file of documents containing facts, figures and statistics from an inquiry which we made not more than two or three years ago into the reasons for rising prices of farm machinery. This government and the previous government did absolutely nothing about that even
March 2, 1S6B

after the committee had made several recommendations that any government could have implemented if it had wanted to.
Unless the minister gives an assurance that he is prepared to do somthing about farm problems there is absolutely no point in the farmers of Canada thinking that anything will be accomplished by agricultural matters being referred to the agricultural committee. When I find that the Minister of Agriculture is not the least bit interested in what is going on in the agricultural committee I am always concerned. I am concerned when the minister sends his parliamentary secretary to see that the committee does not do anything and does not step out of line. His department even sends a sort of adviser to make sure that nothing happens, to make sure that a quorum can be maintained and to see that nothing is slipped in which might accomplish something.
I may be unfair in thinking that previous ministers have not really wanted to do anything about agriculture. I am quite sure that the last two ministers have not really wanted to do anything about agricultural problems. In fact, I thought that the last minister did not understand the problems. A million dollar farmer is not the average farmer that I represent. The problems of the million dollar farmer really do not interest the farmers I am associated with. Their problem is to try to live on $3,500 a year, a level which in some cases they are not even successful in reaching. This is the type of farmer about whom I think we must be concerned. To be successful in dealing with the small farmer's problems we shall have to consider all possible potential means to solve his problems.
The other night I discussed some of the problems facing ARDA. ARDA is not a matter that should come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Forestry. Its problems concern the Minister of Agriculture. The minister is well aware of the long term potential of the ARDA program because in the long run it offers a solution for agriculture. The minister is as well aware as I am that many farmers in Renfrew and Timiskaming should not be on the farms they occupy today. Our problem is to find a solution to get them off the farms without bringing about the bad effects of great dislocations in communities and among the people who are going to be displaced. The solution to this problem will have to be considered over a long term. Standards will have to be set. Surveys will have to be made in the national interest to find out in what areas these displacements must take place.
