[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
This has not been done. Over the years we have given lip service to the ARDA program but we have not really implemented it. We have used it as a patronage machine in Ontario where the provincial government is getting the advantage of the patronage for which the federal government provides the cash. Everyone here knows this is true. That cannot be changed unless the federal government provides leadership in setting out the type of proposals that should be implemented, surveying large areas, and deciding what changes should be made.
At present a member of the provincial legislature can say, It would be very nice to have a little park here and a duck pond there; the federal government will give the money for them and I will get the credit. This is happening everywhere in Ontario. Is this our long term approach to agriculture? I say that if we do not do anything about the long term problem there is no use doing anything about the short term problem because it in fact is dying off.
The average age of farmers in Ontario is well over 50 years. They cannot hire extra labour. Seasonal help is a necessity. The United States government allows transient workers to enter that country from Mexico but as the season advances and those workers reach our borders we do not allow them into Canada because the federal Department of Agriculture has never introduced legislation to allow them to enter on a temporary basis. If we do allow these workers to enter Canada we shall have to make sure our farmers provide them with proper accommodation and wages, but tobacco harvesting, berry picking and other types of seasonal agriculture are capable of providing fairly reasonable salaries.
We have been very interested in the political manipulation of the eastern feed grain agency. I do not know where it stands now but the farm organizations are in favour of it. There is resentment in western Canada about an agency that is going to buy and sell, but the committee which studied this matter took that into consideration. It was quite prepared to have western representatives on the eastern feed grain board to see that an advantage was not established in eastern Canada which would be detrimental to the operations of the Canadian Wheat Board in western Canada.
I do not believe the eastern farmers are interested in gaining an advantage. All they

March 2, 1966
Supply-Agriculture
want is to be protected against the discrimination which hurts them now because of storage problems and the vast difference in the cost of feed grain in eastern Canada compared with the cost in western Canada. There is the cost of moving the grain but the federal government pays for its storage. Yet the grain costs $15 to $20 a ton more during the winter months than in the summer months. The feed grain policy is already established.
I suggest that both the farm machinery problem and the feed grain agency problem will have to be settled by the minister himself. If he refers them to a committee nothing will be done this year and nothing may ever be done about them. Our committee on farm machinery prices sat for four or five months and took a lot of my time and the time of other hon. members but it resulted in absolutely nothing. I may be unfair in saying that because for a four or five month period the farm machinery companies were cautious about raising their prices. However, they made up that time lag once they found out we really did not intend to do anything about the problem except have an inquiry.
The workers of Canada, the white collar people of Canada and even those on pension have decided that the income they receive must be reasonable enough to maintain a decent standard of living. When we find the automobile industry in trouble we give it a $50 million handout. When we find the old age pensioners in trouble we try to give them an extra handout of $25. We are seized of the problems facing most other areas of production in Canada but not in the agricultural area.
We can provide subsidies. I was very interested in the motion moved the other night by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale but I did not participate in the debate because I wanted to see it come to a vote and pass. However, a member from Vancouver, with no knowledge of agriculture at all, spoke on the motion and talked it out. I had hoped it would pass because it would provide an extra 5 or 6 cents a dozen for eggs in western Canada. There, eggs are selling for 17 and 18 cents a dozen, but people in eastern Canada have to pay 75 cents a dozen. Surely we can do something to equalize that situation and see that the producers get a fair percentage of the retail price. However, the motion was talked out.
In my opinion subsidies are not the answer but unless we can devise a better system we

shall have to provide subsidies. If we do there should be a limit so that we do not end up with a vertically integrated industry that will be only a financial operation. If we provide subsidies it should only be done for farmers who are operating efficiently and the subsidies should only be enough to help keep them in production.
We also have need of national marketing legislation because if we introduce a subsidy program and build up production to a reasonable level we are likely to create surpluses and national marketing legislation will be necessary to dispose of them. There is really no surplus agricultural production in the world today. There is a deficit. There is a great need for agricultural products all over the world. Yet Canada and the United States are faced with the problem of providing a decent level of income for the farm community and we have a surplus problem.
We had a surplus problem with wheat which to some extent has been solved. We did not solve it in the old manner of having people come here and buy it. We went out and sold it. It is true there have been disasters throughout the world. It is true the large sale to Russia a couple of years ago was a Godsend to wheat farmers. But people who have been in Russia say that country will need wheat for some years to come and we must do our best to maintain that market.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
This year we will probably not have surpluses in agricultural commodities except with respect to two products. It is hinted that by fall we will have a deficit in butter production and that it may be necessary again to import butter into Canada. If we have to do this, it is an indication that we have not been providing the proper support for the dairy industry; otherwise we would not have found ourselves in this position. There is a potential for almost double the production in the dairy industry if that industry is assured of a market for its products. The support will have to be national in scope because there is a problem between provinces in matters of trade with one province cutting the throat of an adjacent province. This is quite evident in eastern Canada.
There are many other problems in agriculture which we will have to face. In my opinion, before his estimates are passed the minister will have to make a statement in respect of what he intends to do. While he is not really responsible for these estimates, let
March 2, 1966

us not knock them because they did get the former minister of agriculture a seat in the other place. However, I think the minister has an obligation to outline what kind of legislation he proposes because it is not good enough to send the estimates to the standing committee if we are not sure what the minister wants to accomplish. I hope we will have a report from the minister indicating the solutions he has in mind which he hopes parliament will approve in respect of Canada's agricultural problems.

subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall not speak at length on these estimates, since these are last year's estimates and, moreover, it is not even the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) who took part in the implementation of this policy. Therefore, we cannot praise or even less blame him for the deficiencies that might have existed under the former minister.
I shall therefore confine myself to putting a few questions to the minister and telling him that we set all our hopes on him and that we are anxious to take cognizance of his next estimates as soon as possible. I urge all members of the house to pass the remaining estimates of the Minister of Agriculture, so that we may go on to more urgent matters.
Mr. Chairman, if these estimates were to be given the same treatment as those of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin), it would be a second disaster, because it is obvious that the Minister of Justice is now in a dilemma due to the time wasted so as to prevent the house from undertaking more serious work.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) if he will bring forward legislation establishing a Canadian dairy commission this year, in 1966.
We, in Quebec, have long been asking for a Canadian farm products commission for the east. The minister indicated that such legislation is intended. To my mind, this is the first step toward granting us what we have so often been asking for in this house. We ask him to go further in his efforts in this connection, so as to cover not only the dairy industry-I am referring especially to Quebec and the eastern part of the province-but all the various farm products of the province of Quebec, in order that they too may benefit.
For many years western farmers have been benefiting from the advantages offered by the Canadian wheat board. Wheat is their main product, and we are glad for them. On
Supp ly-A griculture
the other hand, the time has come for us, in 1966, to be able to congratulate a Minister of Agriculture who will put before us an act for the setting up of an eastern farm products board.
I told the minister that I would be brief. I shall summarize, because I do not want to take up too much of the time of the house. The second item I wish to deal with is the dairy policy which guarantees a maximum price of $4 per cwt. excluding transportation costs, to all sectors.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Well, there is also a paragraph which must get the minister's attention. Because of the failure last year to add "excluding transportation costs", our Quebec farmers sustained a loss of 20 cents, 22 cents, 23 cents, 24 cents per cwt. of milk, when the government had just decreed a price of $3.50 per cwt. of milk. Therefore, when $4 is mentioned, let it be clear that that $4 will be paid in addition to transportation costs.
In fact, last year, it was realized that the farmer did not get $3.50 any more, but only $3.22, $3.21 and even $3.20, depending on transportation costs. I see the minister making notes. I know that he will take the necessary measures to ensure a fair treatment for all farmers. Some farmers will get $4, while others, not so well located from the transportation point of view, will not get it.
The third point, Mr. Chairman, deals with the Crop Insurance Act, in which we take a strong interest. The government expressed its desire to amend this act, and we are confident that it will be amended so as to allow Quebec farmers to have their share of the benefits of crop insurance which, up to now, has helped only western provinces. I am not blaming the western provinces. On the other hand, one would say that this act was created and intended for western farmers and with a view to western production. Now, in my opinion, this is the reason why this act cannot apply to all Quebec farmers. I did not have any discussion with the Quebec authorities to ascertain why they had not sought to have the benefits of the Crop Insurance Act extended to their farmers, but I think that the Quebec farmers were not included because of the shortcomings of the act.
I point out, at this time, that the act should be amended so as to include not only dairy production and grain, but all crops.
I remind the minister that the Quebec farmers are asking that all the crops be

March 2, 1966
Supply-Agriculture
included in that legislation and also that the indemnity for loss be set at 90 per cent, whatever the cause of the loss.
We know of several causes and, as mentioned a while ago by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), we also learned last year about the rainmaking machines. At first, when we talked about rainmaking machines in the house, most hon. members thought it was funny; those who did not laugh refrained from doing so only because they felt a little sorry for us; others did not believe us at all. Today, all hon. members are convinced that such machines exist and have been operating full time for ten years during the summer. Consequently, it is easier for us today to ask the minister to do something about those rainmaking machines.
When I talk about rainmaking machines, I mean both kinds. As a matter of fact, there are the rainmaking machines on land. They are set up in forests, on farms, on farmers' plots. I am not asking you to legislate about those, because that matter comes under the jurisdiction of the provincial government. But with regard to the seeding of clouds by plane, the federal government must assume its responsibility. In that case, it is a matter of air pollution by plane. I do not know if the federal government can call on some legislation to deal severely with that case. It would have to be very harsh, because some companies would have us walk in swamps to serve bigger interests and not the people.
I previously mentioned in the house some of those interests, particularly the Quebec Hydro which has been letting rain fall on our heads for three years, because it must fill its Manic I, Manic II, Manic III, Manic IV, Manic V dams with 40 per cent of artificial rain. I say that the welfare of the people must come before financial interests, that the health of the people must come before financial health and that our government would do well to pass a law to control the seeding of clouds by plane.
I would also like to deal for a few minutes with the health of animals. Brucellosis has been endemic in our region for two or three years. Well, that epidemic carried away approximately a third of our dairy herds. The government did give the people some compensation but I believe that act is some 20 years old. It is no longer appropriate in view of the current price for stock. In fact, $140 is still given for a purebred dairy cow, whereas a farmer cannot buy one for less than $300; and $70 is given for a cross-breed.

I am therefore humbly suggesting to the minister that the act be amended in order to give $100 for a cross-breed and at least $200 for a purebred dairy cow. It seems to me that would not be exaggerating at all, considering the farmer whose herd is being depleted by that disease. I have seen herds of 50 to 55 heads having to be completely done away with.
And so, if the government gives $200, and the farmer sells the meat of the animal for probably $100 to $125 to a slaughter-house, this will allow the farmer to get $300 and renew his herd without suffering heavy losses. On the other hand, because of all those changes, he will surely not be able to produce before five or six months and he will have to take a loss anyway.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
There is also the question of the farmer's income tax and property taxes. I also want to bring this to the attention of the minister. I have always found it odd, for instance, that paper companies-I mention paper companies because I am more familiar with them-are exempted from the tax on stationary machinery while farm land is taxed to the hilt. This is absurd, because if there is anything stationary in the province of Quebec, and in the country as a whole, it is farm land. Before exempting those big companies from the machinery tax, farm land should be exempted, because, for the farmer, his land is definitely an instrument.
I do not consider the land so much as a real value for the farmer, because if his farm is productive, it is because he cultivates it. Let the farmer leave his farm, as occurs in 40 per cent of the farms in our area abandoned in the last 10, 15 or 20 years, and that farm loses all its value. It can actually be bought for $300 or $400, whereas when the farmer cultivated it, it was valued at $7,000 or $8,000. This shows that the land is only the farmer's tool and that it should be tax-exempt. Let the income be taxed, but stop taxing the landed property which is comparable to the heavy plant of big companies.
I now wish to say a few words about farm credit. If the minister studies the present Farm Credit Act, he will find that it is not at all consistent with the needs of our area.
I do not know what is wrong; I do not know whether this is due to the administrative staff or whether our area is different from the others, but our farmers have a hard time securing a loan under the Farm Credit
March 2, 1966

Act. I think the Minister of Agriculture should investigate.
I found out last year, one case among others, about a farmer, in a position to use easily from $40,000 to $45,000. He has nine lots under cultivation with the most up-to-date machinery. After fighting for a year, do you know how much he got? Ten thousand dollars. Ten thousand dollars were promised to him to build a barn in which milk cows could move about freely. He was given a loan of $10,000 but, a year later, he has yet to receive a cent. I do not know where the trouble lies or whether the federal government is to blame. I do not wish to accuse the minister, because he is new to his job and I know that he wants to improve his department. We saw less of his predecessor and I know that we will see this minister more often. The former minister was thanked by his fellow-citizens because they did not send him back but he was promoted to the Senate by the Liberals. I hope the present minister will start an inquiry. I do noc know whether this depends on the government of the province of Quebec; I do not know what is wrong, but the loans that should be available cannot be obtained in our region.
Those underhand practices must cease. I say "underhand practices" because I hear too much talk on all sides; there is no smoke without fire.
I merely wish to draw to the minister's attention to the Farm Credit Act. If there is a change to be made, an amendment to be brought in, it should be done so that that act can finally be adapted to our area and to the province of Quebec, where farmers who have 300, 400, 600 or 800 acres of cultivated land cannot benefit from the advantages of the act as it now stands.
Once again, I should like to bring to the minister's attention the 25 cents premium per cwt. for the transportation of milk. At the present time, the act provides that the premium may be granted for a minimum production of 10,000 lbs. of producers' milk. I suggest that this is rather high as far as some Quebec producers are concerned. We have some who are producing consumer milk, fluid milk, and others manufacturing milk. They always ship the balance of their manufacturing milk and there are times when they do not have 10,000 lbs. of milk. So they lose the premium on that amount.
Those responsible for paying this premium called me some two or three hours ago to tell
Supply-Agriculture
me that with 9,986 lbs. one could not obtain the subsidy. In my opinion, a slight adjustment to the act would allow all farmers to be treated as fairly as the milk producers.
All in all, those were the remarks I wanted to make, Mr. Chairman.
The member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) said a while ago that there was an agricultural crisis. That is quite true, but I feel it is mainly a crisis of adjustment. Quebec agriculture is going through a period of readjustment, and legislation will simply have to be passed to enable it to adapt itself to the new developments in the farming industry.

subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be very brief because I want to continue the co-operation that our party has shown in trying to get the estimates for 1965-66 through the committee as quickly as possible. I also know we will have an opportunity very soon, or at least I hope so, to question the Minister of Agriculture in the standing committee. At that time we will have an opportunity of discussing with him many of the policies and new programs which I hope he will be bringing in as government policy in keeping with some of the comments the minister made in his opening statement. I want to say also that I congratulate and commend the minister for what I regard as getting right to the nub of the problem in agriculture in that part of his opening statement wherein he suggested that the greatest problem in agriculture is the net income of farmers relative to the incomes of people in other sectors of our economy.
I should like the minister to know that we in this party will give him every co-operation in setting up new policies and programs that will achieve the very desirable end result about which he talked. I say to him as well that when he made his tour of western Canada in early January a number of the statements which the minister made, according to the press, were very well received by western farmers. I know there were some attempts to criticize him and other members of the cabinet after he arrived back in Ottawa in that perhaps he had been a little extreme in his criticism of the railroads with regard to their performance respecting the movement of grain.
I want the minister to know that we in this party support for the most part the criticism he made because we are convinced that here again he got right to the heart of the matter and put his finger on the real problem in so

March 2. 1966
Supply-Agriculture
far as the movement of grain in western Canada is concerned. I shall not go into that matter in great detail today because it was discussed yesterday and on a number of other occasions. But I certainly hope the minister will not be discouraged from pursuing the same line in the future in the interests of the grain producers on the prairies. I would say too, that I believe there was some immediate improvement after these statements were made by a responsible minister of the federal government.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I remember that when the minister made his "some turkey, some plucking" speech in the House of Commons he drew the attention of members to the fact there was an improvement from some 325 or 330 car unloadings in Vancouver per day to 600 per day. I think the Canadian Pacific particularly but the railways generally understand the language of federal ministers when they express their concern in this way. They understand that they need to make an additional effort. I commend the minister for that and, as I said, I hope he will not be discouraged from making other statements of this kind when he sees the need.
I say to the minister with respect to this matter that everyone can understand that during the very short time he was in western Canada he would not have had time to make a personal inspection of the problems and the bottlenecks in the movement of grain. Therefore I think what he was doing was listening to many responsible men in western Canada who are intimately involved in the movement of grain such as the Canadian Wheat Board, the leaders of the wheat pools, the line elevator companies, the heads of terminals and so on.
I believe what the minister was doing was engaging in the same kind of reflection and thinking as these very responsible men and I think this was a good thing. I hope the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Finance to some extent are unable to squelch that kind of attitude.
There are one or two questions I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture because there is some apprehension in the country-perhaps "apprehension" is not the right word-some question in the minds of people about whether or not some of the policies commenced under his predecessor are going to be continued or if some of the plans which

appeared to be under way are going to be carried forward into policies and programs.
One of the questions, is the almost complete reclassification of the various classes at exhibitions so far as prize money is concerned and what the new classes will be. I am not going to go into detail on that now but we would like to know if the present minister intends to carry forward these plans which appeared to be under way. As a matter of fact, there were some changes but all of the changes that were planned had not been made. I understand that there was a meeting in Ottawa within the last few days or the last week at which there was some further discussion. I should like to know what the plans are for the future.
One other thing we would like to know is whether or not the minister intends proceeding with plans to set up a fund from which exhibition corporations can borrow money on a long term basis for the purpose of constructing multiple purpose buildings. There are quite a number of exhibition companies across the country, including the Medicine Hat Exhibition and Stampede Company, who are particularly interested in this plan, and we are still waiting to see whether the federal government is going to set up this fund and make money available on a long term and perhaps low interest basis.
I do not want to keep the committee very long but I want to say to the minister that we in this party believe that the major problem facing Canadian agriculture and all of those who are engaged in it is that our whole price structure is too low and that some policies need to be evolved to improve the structure. We believe that this can probably best be done by an all-party committee that can go into some of these matters in the planning stages rather than always waiting until the government has considered these things and comes before the house with final plans completely worked out. I believe this can be done very effectively if all parties are less interested in who gets the political credit for the actual result of bringing these new policies into effect.
I commend the minister for pointing to this problem in his opening statement and also the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) who spoke and intimated-at least I took this to be so from what he said-that his party was willing to give the kind of co-operation necessary to work out policies so that the whole price structure can be raised. I know that the
March 2, 1S66

Canadian Federation of Agriculture, for example, only a few days ago stated in its brief to the cabinet that even well established farmers are having problems in meeting the so-called cost squeeze. In other words, costs of operation are going up but the receipts are not going up accordingly. This is something that many of us who are well acquainted with agriculture in our constituencies have known for a very long time. Many well established farmers have come to me within the last few months, more than at any time in the past, complaining about the cost-price squeeze. Therefore anything that we in this party can do in co-operation with the government and other opposition parties which will change this situation we certainly intend to do. We believe that some very positive steps can and should be taken respecting a national sugar policy. We also believe that some steps ought to be taken to set up a two price policy for wheat. There seems to be some measure of support for this kind of a program in all corners of this house. We want to co-operate with the minister in completing a new dairy policy for Canada.
I believe that if any plan to raise the whole price structure for farmers is going to succeed it is also going to require some tariff amendments. I do not say that we need them for the purpose of restricting trade but we need some co-operation from the Department of Trade and Commerce and from the government, through instructions to the Tariff Board and so on, to insulate our own domestic markets from the influence of the prices of dumped or surplus products from other countries. This is particularly evident in the price of sugar, turkeys and lamb from time to time as well as potatoes and many other things. We have some legislation at the present time but it is not effective because some of the dumped or surplus products can and do in fact from time to time break down our whole price structure. They affect our whole price structure in a way that bears no relationship to supply and demand within Canada in so far as our own production is concerned.
Therefore it is not a matter of entering into a new round of tariff changes which would be designed to restrict trade but simply a case of protecting our own domestic producers in our own home markets. I think it is fair to say that many of the other countries in the so-called western world have already done this and there would be no problem by
S upply-A griculture
way of retaliatory action from other countries if we did the same thing in self-defence.
In closing I should also like to ask the minister to provide the house with a clearcut statement of policy respecting cost-shared emergency assistance programs in so far as the federal government is concerned. The minister has taken some criticism on the floor of the house respecting this matter during this session. As I said, I do not want to take a lot of time now but there are some provincial governments across the country, particularly Alberta in recent weeks, who seem to think, and I believe with some justification, that the federal government does not have a policy or at least does not have a policy that is consistent for all the provinces. We believe that there should be some statement so the provinces will know what to expect by way of response from the federal government.
We were under the impression for many months that at any time a province set up an emergency assistance program toward which it was prepared to pay 50 per cent of the cost the federal government would match that percentage. We believed this because it had been stated over and over again in the House of Commons by the former minister of agriculture and I think by the Prime Minister on more than one occasion. Therefore we think there is some discrimination on the part of the federal government as to which request it accepts and which it does not. I would ask the minister to provide us with a statement of policy and to apply that policy to all provinces on the same basis.
I am going to conclude my remarks with this very brief statement. I inform the minister that he can expect full co-operation from us in his determination to bring agricultural incomes into line with those in other sectors of our economy. He can also expect co-operation in the Standing Committee on Agriculture if he will come to that committee with his plans and discuss them before they become hard and fast government policy. So far as we are concerned we do not care whether the government or the opposition gets the political credit as long as we do something positive soon to meet the cost-price squeeze which at this time is hurting even well established farmers.

subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will not be long, for I have only a few remarks to make on agriculture.

March 2. 1966
Supply-Agriculture
Mr. Chairman, in view oi the fact that the constituency which I represent is almost exclusively agricultural, I am of the opinion that if agriculture is to prosper, then we must see to it that it be given a framework within which it can endure. A framework must be established for agriculture and it is the government's responsibility to set it up.
I know that the matter of farming is of both provincial and federal jurisdiction, but I also know that the federal government has a large part in it.
When speaking about assisting apgricul-ture, the first thing to do is to establish budgets. I have examined the budget of the Department of Agriculture for the year 1965-66, which totals $121,815,100.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
To distribute among the farmers their share of this budget, considering the cost of administration, we see that there is not much left for the farmer. Almost everything is spent on administration. It is a budget of $125 million, and I will tell you in a few moments how little is spent on agriculture itself.
For instance, if you look at the details of vote No. 1, you will see:
Civil salaries and wages, $54,461,200; Civil Allowances, $169,500; Professional and Special services, $2,607,700; Travelling and Removal expenses, $3,522,100; Freight, Express and Cartage, $228,400; Postage, $124,800; Telephones, Telegrams and other Communications media, $458,600; Publication of Reports and other Material, $520,000; Exhibit Material, Advertising, Films, Radio and Displays, $150,400; Office Stationery, Supplies and Equipment, $1,276,500; Materials and Supplies, $3,626,300; Construction or Acquisition of Buildings and Works, including lands, $31,602,000; Construction or Acquisition of Equipment, $2,698,900; Repairs and Upkeep, $932,600; Rental, $97,700; Town Services, $1,019,400;
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it cost nearly $100 million to distribute $121,815,100; there remains $15 million for agricultural purposes.
Can agriculture really be assisted, with such an administration? The minister will have to look into the cost of administration. The trouble, in all this, is administration. The cost of administration is tremendous. If it cost $100 million to distribute $15 million, 1 say to the Minister of Agriculture-I know very well that it is not his fault because he has not always been there-that it is his responsibility to correct this anomaly in administration.
If it is going to cost $100 million to distribute $14 million to the farmers, I think that other ways would cost much less. Right now, it does not make sense.
[Mr. Latulippe.l
If agriculture is going to be organized, money must first be distributed to farmers.
In my riding, for instance, 60 per cent of farm loans are turned down; all those who ask for $5,000, $10,000, $8,000, $4,000, cannot obtain them; all are refused. Many loans of $15,000, $18,000, $20,000, are also refused.
There is no money left to help the farmer; all is spent on administration.
When agricultural reform is mentioned, we are referred to ARDA which covers another area. ARDA was supposed to solve every problem, but ARDA has not solved anything up to now. If I had the figures with me on ARDA administration, you would be surprised at the cost of administering this organization from which farmers hardly get any benefit.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
We are being told that in the province of Quebec, the farm income is 30 per cent lower than in other provinces. This is ridiculous. Steps will have to be taken by all means so that farmers may take advantage of their production or derive a profit from it. The farmer would not need the government so much if he had an income, but he has not. He manufactures for less than the cost price and he is not the one who prices his products. Most of the time, when he has a product to sell, its price is established by other organizations beyond his control.
With regard to feed grain, I must say that I have been sitting in the house for three years and during this period, farmers have been submitting briefs to us and asking us to see to it that they obtain feed grain at a reasonable price. The price of feed grain is too high; the implementation of the program is too costly. The farmer does not benefit from it, because he pays too much for the feed grain he needs.
They recently presented a brief in which they request the setting up of an eastern feed board and ask the minister if anything has been done in that respect. I do not know if it will do any good. If the administration costs are as high as in all the other departments, it will not be worth anything. On the other hand, if costs are kept down to a minimum, it might be useful to the farmer.
In their brief, the farmers also say that Canada will be short 500 million pounds of milk this year.
Farmers are giving up the land and dairy herds because there is no money in it. They are asking for a cost price of $4 per cwt. of industrial milk.
March 2, 1966

When we ask questions in the house, we are told to put them on the order paper, because they are of a general character. Therefore, today I will ask the Minister of Agriculture a question. Is he willing to see to it that the farmers will get the price they are asking for, that is $4 per cwt., to allow them to make a small profit, to encourage them and to enable them to meet their needs?
I would like to deal with all kinds of things, but I do not want to take too much time.
With regard to the cost of machinery, farmers are complaining that it is too expensive, that there are too many taxes on machinery. I ask the Minister of Agriculture to consult with his colleagues, especially the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), to see if a way can be found to manufacture farm machinery cheaply. The first thing to do is to remove all taxes on that machinery.
The government should also be asked for subsidies to help the farmers. If it really wants to do something for the farmers, it should grant subsidies on farm machinery. It would cost less to finance farm machinery than defence equipment. A tank costs a million dollars, if not more. With the price of a tank, several pieces of farm equipment and tractors could be manufactured; they would help agriculture and be useful. It would be much less expensive for the government to manufacture farm machinery than cannons, tanks or war equipment which will never serve.
If we want to fight poverty, we must not forget that poverty prevails in farming. If we make farming prosperous, all the other classes of society, as well as the country's economy in general, will be prosperous. The farmer is the greatest consumer in Canada. He buys all sorts of things and has varied needs . The farmer is an important factor-the most important one-of Canadian industry. Let agriculture prosper and so will Canada's economy.
The Minister of Agriculture should press the Minister of Finance to abolish the famous 11 per cent tax on the farmer's building materials. Farmers are always building. They need all sorts of buildings. They build "terrible" buildings, and this tax is put on their building materials. The farmers are in a state of stagnation. Let the necessary pressures be applied in order to abolish this famous 11 per cent tax.
Supply-Agriculture
Mr. Chairman, I could say a lot more. For example, I mentioned earlier the agricultural loans which are refused. There is much to be done in this respect. Inquiries must be made. That would not be difficult because the farm loan board does not have too many offices in the province of Quebec and in Canada. The minister has only to ask those officers if he wants to find out the percentage of loans that were refused.
There are many farmers who, thanks to a small loan of $5,000, $6,000 or $10,000, could buy more land, improve their farm buildings and remain there for quite a while yet. But they abandon their farms because they are refused such a loan.
In the last five years, 60 per cent of the farms have been abandoned in a certain part of my riding. Every day, those who remain are like the bird in the tree. They want to go because they are not making any money. It does not pay.
We expect a lot from the minister. We realize he is new at the job, but we know he is eager to help. I wish to congratulate him and thank him for the interest and goodwill he has shown towards the farm people. I am sure he will do his duty and provide agriculture with services that will really help the farmer while promoting the growth of the farming industry.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this first opportunity to offer my most sincere congratulations to the new Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) on his appointment. As he has found, we, on this side of the house, have no objection to the Minister of Agriculture coming from either the east or the west, from the province of Quebec or the Maritimes. What we want is a Minister of Agriculture who keeps his eyes open, cocks his ears and is ready to accept suggestions from members of rural constituencies in this house.
Therefore, we are proud to have, at the head of the Department of Agriculture, a minister from the east, but I should like at the same time to tell the Minister of Agriculture to ask his colleagues, particularly some of them, not to indulge in partisan politics and not to place too much reliance of the fact that we have an eastern Minister of Agriculture who speaks French-I congratulate the Minister on this-in order to believe

March 2. 1966
Supply-Agriculture
that they will win the support of all the farmers in eastern Canada.
I do not want to refer in any way to certain words of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette). It is not enough to have a Minister of Agriculture from the east who speaks French, we also need a Minister of Agriculture who can take in hand the future of agriculture in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, before resinning my seat, I should like to say a few words about the Canadian dairy commission. Last year, the Minister of Agriculture announced that the Canadian government would, at the first opportunity-this was on March 26, 1965-introduce a bill to establish a Canadian dairy commission. According to the minister, the commission would work in co-operation with the provinces and look after general relations between the government and the dairy industry.
Mr. Chairman, that was on March 26, 1965, and the government was then getting the bill ready for early presentation; this is March 2, 1966, and it has not been introduced yet.
Questions are being raised and I shall put them myself to the minister. Will this Canadian dairy commission to be able to ensure to milk producers a uniform price for milk? In other words, will the milk producer who has no possibility whatsoever to make cheese, powdered milk or butter with his milk, be able to obtain the same price as the one who ships his milk to another factory? This is very important. Whether it be a producer who ships his milk to a cheese factory, a butter factory or a processing plant, or a farmer who manufactures milk powder, skim milk or casein, I feel that such farmer should be paid the same price as the other farmers in his area.
So, I ask the minister: Will the Canadian dairy commission ensure that all milk producers in Canada will receive a uniform price?
My second question: Will the Canadian dairy commission exert a deep influence on milk quality?
I have only a few words to say on this, Mr. Chairman. You have, for instance, a farmer who ships his milk and does all he can to have a clean and excellent milk production. If his neighbour or second neighbour produces an inferior milk, the price of this good farmer will decrease because his neighbour or second neighbour produces milk of an inferior quality.
Will the proposed Canadian dairy commission try to diversify production as much as possible all year round to encourage farmers to produce more milk during the winter months? That is very important for the future of the Canadian dairy industry.
Fourth question:	Will the commission
definitively deal with this question of milk transportation?
Supply-Agriculture
In my province, as I believe is the case in other provinces in Canada, milk is widely transported.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
There is milk that is carried 100, 200 and 300 miles every day. In the province of Quebec, you have milk which leaves Sherbrooke to be sold in Montreal and from there it goes to Trois-Rivieres and then on to Quebec city. Milk goes from one place to another just like that and who is paying? Once again, it is the farmer.
The Canadian dairy commission will have to co-ordinate milk transportation to ensure that the producer will get the highest possible income and that 25 or 35 cents per cwt. will not be spent for nothing.
Fifth question regarding the Canadian dairy commission: Will it make a lot of publicity to promote dairy product consumption?
Sixth question: Will the commission deal with dairy product exports?
In 1900, 1901 and 1902, Canada exported more than 100 million pounds of cheese annually to England, and the minister can check these figures if he wants to. Today, Canada is producing about 130 million pounds of cheese and exports only 30 million pounds. Now, cheese really sells at a good price in England.
Seventh question: Will the Canadian dairy commission have a part to play in the importation of milk products in Canada, such as the cheese being imported at present, and also in the case of butter which will eventually have to be imported within a few months or a year, because butter will probably be scarce in Canada?
Those are questions which we are asking and to which we should like to get answers.
We should like to know whether the Canadian dairy commission will try to find answers to those seven specific questions I have raised.
Mr. Chairman, I shall now conclude my remarks by reminding the minister that the dairy industry is of the greatest importance to eastern farmers. It is imperative, this year, that we get for our dairy producers, who are insisting upon it-and it is only normal-a minimum price of $4 per cwt. for all industrial milk.

I know the minister is very sympathetic to this subject and I am sure he will do what he can to influence his colleagues to take some action. Putting it very briefly and bluntly, the dairy farmers of Ontario must in some way or other be guaranteed a minimum of $4 per hundred pounds for their milk regardless of where that milk goes. This is essential because the income of all other groups in the community, including labour, management, service jobs and the professions, has gone up. I know that some of the government members from Toronto and Montreal will suggest that they are paying more for milk and that

March 2. 1966

may be true, but it is the large dairies such as Bordens and others which are receiving the extra amount of money rather than the dairy farmers.
Another popular misconception is that the farmers who have fluid milk contracts-for the benefit of city members, that refers to milk used for drinking-receive $5 per hundred pounds of milk. That is true in respect of the amount of milk they sell for fluid purposes but for much of their milk they receive only about $2.60 per hundred pounds because the amount of milk produced over and above their fluid contracts goes for manufacturing purposes.
There is one other thing I should like to say for the record. As has been pointed out in some newspapers, farm income for 1963 was up 13 per cent. That is true, if statistics can prove anything, but not true in respect of all farmers. I may say that statistics would indicate that the income of farmers on the prairies has increased 30.5 per cent. That is fine and we are all delighted to see that the people in the west are doing so well because in past years they had the tough end of the stick, but so far as Ontario farmers are concerned their income in 1964 was down 7.1 per cent from 1963. I think if we remove specialized crops from that figure, such as tobacco and fruits, we will find that the income of the Ontario dairy farmer was down even more than 7.1 per cent.
It is up to any government to make sure that the various groups in our society get their fair share of our buoyant prosperity, but the dairy farmers are not receiving their share. In fact, they are losing money. In this regard I am sure the minister is aware of a most dangerous situation, namely, that dairy farmers are giving up, selling their herds and getting off the farms altogether because they cannot make ends meet. Unless something is done soon-perhaps deficiency payments may be the best answer-to increase to $4 per hundred pounds of milk the price paid to Ontario dairy farmers, there will develop a serious situation. I think something in this regard must be done by the minister, his colleagues and his administrative staff as soon as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I think I should briefly answer the hon. member in this regard. In so far as national marketing policies are concerned, in the short time I have been with the department I have found it to be one of the areas of very grave difficulty because, as the hon. member knows, the Privy Council in the 1930's decided that agricultural marketing was a provincial and not a federal matter. I think that in the east in particular farmers are very much taken with the example of the wheat board and feel that if they could market on a national basis in a manner analogous to what the wheat board has been able to do for the western wheat producer, their marketing procedures would be more effective and beneficial.
Bearing in mind the constitutional difficulties, I am very hopeful that the approach of a national dairy commission, which I think will be a successful advent in regard to marketing in this area, will lead to a solution of this problem. This can only be done in conjunction with provincial agencies such as the Ontario Milk Marketing Board which was set up last fall. As the hon. member may have noticed, in the speech from the throne in the province of Quebec it was announced that they are going to set up a provincial milk marketing board.
It would be my hope that this general pattern of provincial boards working in conjunction with and under the aegis of a federal board could achieve all the benefits of national marketing. But there would have to be a provincial-federal meeting of minds in this area before it could become possible. I
Supply-Agriculture
am very hopeful that in the dairy industry we will be able to achieve this and that a national dairy commission working in conjunction with provincial marketing agencies will set the pattern for national marketing to which I believe my hon. friend is referring. It may be that if this pattern is successful it could well be continued in other spheres and areas of agricultural products to give the agricultural producer the kind of stability and certainty of price that he needs if he is to be able to afford to form the sort of economically viable unit which will be productive and rewarding in the future.
With respect to the committee's consideration in these areas I think, with respect, it would be presumptuous of me to tell the committee what to do, what studies to make or the areas in which they should involve themselves. I can only assure the hon. member and the committee that certainly I and my officials will be only too pleased to appear before the committee and discuss any of these matters that the committee wishes to discuss, subject always to the rules which prevent our disclosing legislation that is in the mill. Contrary to what hon. members opposite may believe, my colleagues in the cabinet are kindly, benign, delightful gentlemen, and I can assure you they would do anything they could to help anyone in trouble.

Therefore the entire P.F.A.A. area was covered by emergency payments. There was no preferring of one area over another, and I might point out that in the province of Manitoba, in their administration of the 1959 program, they specifically did not pay anyone who had received P.F.A.A. They took exactly the same view as we find we must take in this case.
I have repeatedly sought a way-and I point no finger at anyone because I have been no wiser than anyone else in this regard-to see if we could make a contribution without in fact preferring several P.F.A.A. areas over the rest of the P.F.A.A. areas, many of which had also suffered losses for more than three years in a row. This is the quandary with which I am faced and I have not been able to find a way around it.
Many of the questions asked have been to this effect: Has there been any request from the provincial government for aid in this emergency which would not in fact be a payment supplementary to P.F.A.A. payments, thus preferring one, two or three P.F.A.A. areas over others? I have had no request in line with this approach. Had we had such requests, so that in fact it was not a preferring of some P.F.A.A. areas over others, and if there was some other method of handling it, then it might well be we could participate; but I do not see how we can discriminate against certain P.F.A.A. areas as compared with others.

suffered for more than the three years. This is a quandary. I appreciate very much the hon. member's sincerity, and I only regret I have not been able to figure a way around the problem.

Mr. Chairman, I want to congratulate the minister on his appointment to the agricultural portfolio, and his trip throughout western Canada, during which time certain statements were made to the effect that it was unfortunate the government had no representation in the province of Saskatchewan.
Let me assure the minister that I will co-operate with him at all times in attempting to improve the agricultural situation in the province of Saskatchewan. Specifically I should like to deal with the matter of terminal elevators in western Canada. Many of these elevators are sitting empty. I have placed several questions on the order paper pertaining to this elevator operation, and I had hoped that some of these questions might have been answered before now. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture is interested in the items to which I have referred in my questions.
In the western part of this country we refer to these elevators as great white elephants. As an example of why this is so, let me refer to an empty elevator in my riding with a capacity of 5,500,000 bushels, which has modern drying and cleaning facilities. This is the type of thing which leads us to refer to these elevators in the way I have indicated.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to take up much of the minister's time, but I do suggest he look into this situation and use his influence to correct it. I know the minister realizes that the farmers must get their wheat off their land on quotas, and can do so only by putting pressure on the wheat board and the railways to move it from these elevators. When this happens we always get the runaround and are told that for this or that

March 2. 1966
Supply-Agriculture
reason it cannot be done. I urge the minister to take a good look at the situation with regard to these terminal elevators. Let us make some use of them. We pay large staffs to sit there and do very little if anything. I realize these people have to be kept on but the elevators should be used for the purpose for which whey were intended, that is storage.
I realize also that other questions enter into this matter. There is the question of drop-off charges, and so on. These charges are given as an excuse for the final payment in regard to wheat being something similar to that paid last year, which constituted a drop of 10 or 15 cents a bushel. I maintain that we are paying a permanent staff to operate these elevators, the facilities are there and they should be used. These are Canadian government elevators and if the grain was put into them and no charge was made for storage the situation would be no different than it is at present, when employees are sitting there year after year and no grain is going through the elevators.
I am not saying this is the situation in all elevators but it is the situation in two or three elevators which I have investigated and which are empty at the present time. Last year when the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and myself put some pressure on the government to have some grain put into them at the end of July, 238,000 bushels of wheat were put into one of the elevators but it was taken out again within two or three weeks. At the present time we have a 5J million bushel capacity elevator in the city of Moose Jaw that does not have a bushel of grain in it. I do not say this situation exists in regard to other elevators because I have not the figures before me, but if it is the case I think the Minister of Agriculture should take a good, hard look at this situation and see what can be done about it.
I would draw another matter to the attention of the minister. It may not come under this item but perhaps the minister would bear with me for a moment. I would ask the minister to use his influence with the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue in this regard. I am referring again to the question of storage. Under a bill that was passed last year-this came under the

eastern feed grain policy, I believe-a farmer who built storage facilities was eligible for a 25 per cent write-off on them if they were built between May 1, 1965, and December 31, 1966. The Minister of Agriculture should take a good, hard look at this situation and use his influence with his colleagues in the cabinet to have this program put on a permanent basis. I am sure it would help all the farmers of Canada a great deal.
